lessons.title: Kleiner, schneller, billiger: the comparative
lessons.goal: Compare two phones, apps or people in one sentence with the comparative and als.

grammar.point: The comparative is the adjective + -er (klein, kleiner). A few short words also get an Umlaut (alt, älter). To say than, use als: thing 1 + ist + comparative + als + thing 2.
grammar.oneLine: Mein Handy ist kleiner als dein Handy. Adjective + er, then als.

mistake.wrong: Mein Handy ist kleiner wie dein Handy.
mistake.right: Mein Handy ist kleiner als dein Handy.
mistake.why: After a comparative German uses als for than. Wie is only for things that are equal (so klein wie), which you learn in lesson 3.

terms.meaning: the form of an adjective that says more, for example kleiner (smaller)
the two dots on a, o or u (ä, ö, ü) that change the vowel sound
the word for than in a comparison

cards.title: Before we start: which one is better?
cards.body: Welcome to chapter 3, Immer online? The WG compares phones, apps, series and films, talks about screen time and goes to the cinema. First you need one tool for every comparison: Mein Handy ist kleiner als dein Handy. You already know a small piece of it, because lieber means more gladly.
steps: You already know: gern and lieber from A2 chapter 1, and adjectives like klein and schnell.
New today: the comparative, adjective + er, and als for than.
By the end you can: compare two phones, apps or people in one sentence.

examples.de: Mein Handy ist klein.
examples.en: My phone is small.
examples.why: You know this already.

examples.de: Mein Handy ist kleiner als dein Handy.
examples.en: My phone is smaller than your phone.
examples.why: New today: kleiner = klein + er, and als = than.

cards.more: Think of a seesaw. When two things sit on it, one goes up and one goes down. Your phone is on one side, your friend's phone on the other. In English you add -er (smaller) and say than. German does the same job: you add -er to the adjective, and you say als. That is the whole idea. The next cards show it in small steps: first the -er, then als, then what changes with verbs, questions and a few short words with dots (Umlaut).

cards.title: lieber is already a comparative
cards.body: You know gern (gladly) and lieber (more gladly). Lieber is the comparative of gern: the form that says more. It looks different, but it does the same job as the -er in kleiner. Klein becomes kleiner, schnell becomes schneller.
cards.lead: The introduction showed kleiner next to klein. First, a small surprise: you already used a comparative, the word lieber, when you said what you prefer.

examples.de: Ben liest gern.
examples.en: Ben likes reading.

examples.de: Ben liest lieber Zeitungen.
examples.en: Ben prefers reading newspapers.

examples.de: Anna hört lieber Radio.
examples.en: Anna prefers listening to the radio.

deeper.text: German uses the same comparative for adjectives and for adverbs like gern, so schnell can describe a phone or a runner. English splits them: fast and faster, but well and better. Lieber is an irregular one, because lieber is not gern plus -er. Lesson 2 collects all the irregular forms in one table, so you only need to meet them once.

example.de: Mira trinkt lieber Tee.
example.en: Mira prefers to drink tea.

cards.more: A ladder has steps. Step one is gern, a little bit nice. Step two is lieber, nicer. German adjectives work on the same ladder: klein is the bottom step, kleiner is one step up. Every time you want to say more, you put -er at the end of the word. Gern is a special one because its step two looks different, but you already know it, so you are halfway there.

cards.title: Make the comparative in two steps
cards.body: Step 1: take the adjective. Step 2: add -er. Klein becomes kleiner. Words that end in -el lose the e before the l: dunkel becomes dunkler. Teuer is the other one to learn: teurer. Words that end in -e only add -r: leise becomes leiser. Moderner and spannender just add -er.
cards.lead: You saw that -er means more. Now you learn the exact recipe, so you can build the comparative of almost every adjective yourself.

examples.de: Mein Handy ist schneller.
examples.en: My phone is faster.

examples.de: Der Fernseher ist moderner.
examples.en: The television is more modern.

examples.de: Das Zimmer ist dunkler.
examples.en: The room is darker.

deeper.text: Why does the e drop? Dunkeler would have two weak e sounds in a row, so speakers shorten it to dunkler. The same happens with teuer and teurer. Adjectives that end in -d or -t, like spannend, are fine: they just add -er, and the d stays. Be careful with -er words in general: modern is not shortened, so it is moderner.

example.de: Die Serie ist spannender.
example.en: The series is more exciting.

cards.more: Imagine the adjective is a train and -er is one more carriage. Most trains take the carriage with no trouble: klein plus er. A few trains already have a little e in the back that is in the way. The e jumps off and the carriage hooks on: dunkel becomes dunkler. If the train already ends in -e (leise), you only add the r. You just add a bit and you are done.
steps: Step 1: take the adjective: klein.
Step 2: add -er: kleiner.
Check the ending: -el drops the e (dunkel, dunkler); teuer becomes teurer; -e only adds -r (leise, leiser).

cards.title: als means than
cards.body: To compare two things, use als. The pattern is: thing 1 + ist + comparative + als + thing 2. Thing 2 has the same job as thing 1, so after ist it is also in the nominative, the subject form: als ich, als er, als das Handy. Als is a conjunction.
cards.lead: You can now make kleiner and teurer. On this card you learn how to say what you compare it with, so one sentence holds both things.

examples.de: Mein Handy ist kleiner als dein Handy.
examples.en: My phone is smaller than your phone.

examples.de: Mira ist schneller als ich.
examples.en: Mira is faster than me.

examples.de: Ich bin langsamer als er.
examples.en: I am slower than him.

deeper.text: English says than me, German says als ich. Thing 2 copies the case of thing 1: both are subjects of ist, so ich, er and sie are right and mich or ihn are wrong. Many learners say mich because English does. Test it with the full sentence: faster than I am. There I is the subject, so German uses ich too.

example.de: Du bist lauter als er.
example.en: You are louder than him.

cards.more: Als is a little bridge between two things. On the left bank stands thing one, on the right bank thing two. The comparative sits in the middle and says which one is bigger, faster or cheaper. Both things do the same job for ist, so they look the same: Mira ist schneller als ich. Think of als as a plus sign with an arrow: it points to the thing you measure against.
steps: Step 1: thing 1 and ist: Mein Handy ist.
Step 2: the comparative: kleiner.
Step 3: als and thing 2: als dein Handy.

cards.title: The comparative after other verbs
cards.body: The comparative is not only for ist. It also goes after an action verb and tells how someone does it: Ben arbeitet schneller als Leon. The form is the same as after ist: the adjective with -er, then als. The comparative stands before als.
cards.lead: So far every comparison used ist. Now you meet the same -er after normal verbs, so you can compare how people do things.

examples.de: Ben arbeitet schneller als Leon.
examples.en: Ben works faster than Leon.

examples.de: Leon liest langsamer als Anna.
examples.en: Leon reads more slowly than Anna.

examples.de: Anna spricht leiser als Mira.
examples.en: Anna speaks more quietly than Mira.

deeper.text: In English you must change the adjective to an adverb: slow becomes slowly. In German there is no change at all. Schnell is the same word in Das Handy ist schnell and Ben arbeitet schnell. That is one thing fewer to remember, and it works for the comparative too.

example.de: Herr Ali kocht schneller als ich.
example.en: Herr Ali cooks faster than I do.

cards.more: Imagine two runners. You do not say a new word for how they run; you say the same word, schnell, for the runner and for the running. In German an adjective can be a describing word for a thing (Das Handy ist schnell) and for an action (Ben arbeitet schnell). It never changes. So adding -er works in both places in the same way: Ben arbeitet schneller als Leon.

cards.title: Negation and questions
cards.body: Make a comparison negative with nicht before the comparative: Das Handy ist nicht billiger als der Laptop. For a yes-or-no question put ist first: Ist der Laptop teurer als der Fernseher? Everything else stays the same.
cards.lead: You can say what is faster or cheaper. Now you learn to say it is not, and to ask the question, which you need for real conversations about phones.

examples.de: Ist der Laptop teurer als der Fernseher?
examples.en: Is the laptop more expensive than the television?

examples.de: Das Handy ist nicht billiger als der Laptop.
examples.en: The phone is not cheaper than the laptop.

examples.de: Ist dein Handy schneller als mein Handy?
examples.en: Is your phone faster than my phone?

deeper.text: For a question with a question word, put the word first and keep the comparative: Was ist teurer, der Laptop oder der Fernseher? This works because the verb stays in position two. Notice that you answer with the same words: Der Laptop ist teurer.

example.de: Was ist billiger, der Laptop oder der Fernseher?
example.en: What is cheaper, the laptop or the television?

cards.more: Picture a light switch with three settings. Statement: the sentence goes in the normal order, thing, ist, comparative, als, thing. Question: you flip ist to the front, like moving a lamp to the top shelf. Negative: you put nicht in front of the comparative, like a sticker that says not. The comparison itself never moves: the comparative, als and the second thing stay together every time.

rows: Der Laptop ist teurer als der Fernseher.
Ist der Laptop teurer als der Fernseher?
Der Laptop ist nicht teurer als der Fernseher.

cards.title: Short adjectives with an Umlaut
cards.body: Some short, common adjectives also add an Umlaut (two dots) when they get -er: alt becomes älter, jung becomes jünger, lang becomes länger, kurz becomes kürzer, stark becomes stärker, schwach becomes schwächer, warm becomes wärmer. Learn these seven as a group.
cards.lead: You know the two steps. Now you learn seven common words that also change their vowel, so you do not say the wrong form like alter or warmer.

examples.de: Ben ist älter als Mira.
examples.en: Ben is older than Mira.

examples.de: Mein Ladekabel ist kürzer als dein Ladekabel.
examples.en: My charging cable is shorter than your charging cable.

examples.de: Heute ist es wärmer als gestern.
examples.en: Today it is warmer than yesterday.

deeper.text: The Umlaut is a sound change that German has kept from old times. Not every adjective gets it: klein just becomes kleiner, and its vowel is ei. These seven are the most common, but a few more behave the same, for example kalt, kälter. Groß also changes, to größer, but it comes in the next lesson with the other special forms. When you meet a new adjective, check the comparative in a dictionary.

example.de: Leon ist jünger als Anna.
example.en: Leon is younger than Anna.

cards.more: Picture the vowel as a person standing straight. In these seven words, when the -er carriage arrives, the vowel leans over and puts on a hat with two dots: a becomes ä. The English words are old, young, long, short, strong, weak, warm. Say the list aloud three times and your ear learns it. The usual mistake is alter instead of älter. The fix: put the dots on.

lessons.title: Gut, besser, mehr: irregular comparatives
lessons.goal: Compare quality, amounts and sizes with the most common irregular comparatives: besser, mehr, lieber, höher, näher, größer.

grammar.point: Seven common words have their own comparative: gut besser, viel mehr, gern lieber, hoch höher, nah näher, groß größer, alt älter. Mehr and weniger never get an ending.
grammar.oneLine: Mein Handy ist besser als dein Handy. Gut has its own form: besser.

mistake.wrong: Mein Handy ist guter als dein Handy.
mistake.right: Mein Handy ist besser als dein Handy.
mistake.why: Gut is irregular: its comparative is besser, never guter. The same is true in English: good, better, not gooder.

terms.meaning: a word that does not follow the normal rule, so you learn its own form
the form of an adjective that says more, for example besser (better)

cards.title: Before we start: not every word follows the rule
cards.body: Last time you made kleiner and schneller with -er. But try it with gut and you get guter, and that is wrong. A few of the most common words are irregular, so you say besser. You hear them every day: Ist das besser? Hast du mehr Zeit? Today you learn them as one small group.
steps: You already know: adjective + er and als, for example Mein Handy ist kleiner als dein Handy.
New today: the irregular comparatives besser, mehr, höher, näher and größer.
By the end you can: compare quality and amounts, for example Mein Handy ist besser als dein Handy.

examples.de: Mein Handy ist kleiner als dein Handy.
examples.en: My phone is smaller than your phone.
examples.why: You know this already.

examples.de: Mein Handy ist besser als dein Handy.
examples.en: My phone is better than your phone.
examples.why: New today: gut becomes besser, not guter.

cards.more: Think of a school class. Most pupils follow the same morning routine: wake up, wash, eat, go. That is the -er rule. But a few pupils, the old friends of the class, do it their own way. They have been around so long that they kept their own style. Gut, viel, hoch, nah and groß are those old friends: you use them all the time, so they keep their own forms. The good news is that there are only a few, and you learn them one card at a time.

cards.title: gut becomes besser
cards.body: Gut (good) does not become guter. It has its own form: besser (better). Use it exactly like kleiner: thing 1 + ist + besser + als + thing 2. It also works after other verbs: Ben kocht besser als ich.
cards.lead: The introduction showed that the -er rule has exceptions. The first and most useful one is gut, because you will say better all the time when you compare phones and apps.

examples.de: Mein Handy ist besser als dein Handy.
examples.en: My phone is better than your phone.

examples.de: Die App ist besser als das Computerspiel.
examples.en: The app is better than the computer game.

examples.de: Ben kocht besser als ich.
examples.en: Ben cooks better than I do.

deeper.text: Besser is also a word on its own, not only half of a comparison. Natives say Das ist besser so (that is better this way), Es geht mir besser (I feel better now) and Gute Besserung (get well soon), where Besserung comes from the same family. English hides this link, but in German besser, Besserung and bessern all belong together. You will hear besser constantly in daily talk.

example.de: Leon spielt besser als Ben.
example.en: Leon plays better than Ben.

cards.more: Gut is a bit like an old shoe that does not need a new sole. English does the same: good does not become gooder, it becomes better. The rule in your mind is: if the English word has a different comparative (good, better), the German one probably does too. Gut, besser. You use besser with als, just like kleiner: Mein Handy ist besser als dein Handy.

cards.title: viel becomes mehr
cards.body: Viel (much, a lot) becomes mehr (more). Wenig (little) becomes weniger (less). Both go before a noun and never get an ending: mehr Zeit, mehr Fotos, weniger Zeit. Mehr and weniger need no -er rule at all.
cards.lead: Besser covered quality. Now you learn how to compare amounts, so you can say who takes more photos or who has less time.

examples.de: Ich mache mehr Fotos als Ben.
examples.en: I take more photos than Ben.

examples.de: Leon hat mehr Zeit als Mira.
examples.en: Leon has more time than Mira.

examples.de: Anna hat weniger Zeit als Ben.
examples.en: Anna has less time than Ben.

deeper.text: English splits its words for less: fewer for things you can count (fewer apps) and less for the rest (less time). German keeps it simpler. Mehr and weniger work for both: mehr Zeit, mehr Fotos, weniger Zeit, weniger Apps. The word before it can change, though: viel Zeit for something uncountable, but viele Fotos for plural things. In the comparative both just become mehr, with no ending.

example.de: Ben hat mehr Apps als ich.
example.en: Ben has more apps than I do.

cards.more: Imagine a glass of water. Viel is the full glass and mehr is the glass after you pour a bit more. Weniger is the glass after you drink some. The glass never changes its shape: it is always the same word, mehr, no matter what is in it (Zeit, Fotos, Kaffee). Mehr is the easiest comparative in the language: there is nothing to add. And mehrere (several) is a different word; if you mean more, say mehr only.

cards.title: gern becomes lieber
cards.body: Gern (gladly) becomes lieber (more gladly, rather). It sits where gern sits, right after the verb: Ich sehe lieber fern. No als is needed to say what you prefer.
cards.lead: Gut and viel changed completely. A third irregular pair is an old friend from chapter 1: gern and lieber, which you can use for what you like to do.

examples.de: Ich sehe lieber fern.
examples.en: I prefer to watch TV.

examples.de: Mira hört lieber Musik.
examples.en: Mira prefers to listen to music.

examples.de: Leon spielt lieber Fußball.
examples.en: Leon prefers to play football.

deeper.text: Lieber is also a small reply on its own. Someone offers you coffee and you say Lieber Tee, I would rather have tea. Or you answer an invitation with Lieber nicht, I would rather not. Both are very natural and polite. Lieber has one more life: in letters, Lieber Ben starts a letter to a man, where it means dear. Same spelling, different job: after the verb it is the comparative of gern.

example.de: Möchtest du Kaffee? – Lieber Tee.
example.en: Would you like coffee? – Rather tea.

cards.more: Gern, lieber, am liebsten is like a volume knob for liking. Gern is a little bit, lieber is more, and am liebsten is the full turn. English has the same idea with like, prefer, like best. In German you only need one small word each time and you put it right after the verb. It is the same slot where gern lived in chapter 1, so you already know where to put lieber.

cards.title: hoch, nah, groß: three small changes
cards.body: Three more adjectives change a little. Hoch becomes höher: the c is gone and there are two dots. Nah becomes näher: two dots. Groß becomes größer: two dots and the ß stays. Say them aloud: höher, näher, größer.
cards.lead: Besser, mehr and lieber changed completely. These three are easier: you keep most of the word and only change a little.

examples.de: Der Turm ist höher als das Haus.
examples.en: The tower is higher than the house.

examples.de: Der Supermarkt ist näher als der Bahnhof.
examples.en: The supermarket is nearer than the station.

examples.de: Ben ist größer als Mira.
examples.en: Ben is taller than Mira.

deeper.text: English uses tall for people and high for towers. German splits them the same way: it uses groß for people and hoch for towers, mountains and prices. Ben ist größer als Mira says Ben is taller, and Der Turm ist höher als das Haus compares heights of buildings. Mixing them up sounds odd. Also note that hoch has no c in its comparative, so you always write höher, never höcher.

example.de: Anna ist größer als Leon.
example.en: Anna is taller than Leon.

cards.more: These three are cousins of the Umlaut group from last time: they get two dots, so they feel familiar. Only hoch is a little sneaky: it also loses the c, so hoch becomes höher, not höcher. Say all three: hoch, höher. nah, näher. groß, größer. The table shows the whole story in one line each. When you build the sentence, you use them like kleiner: add als and the second thing.

rows: the c drops, dots on o

cards.title: The irregular comparatives in one table
cards.body: Here are all the irregular comparatives of the chapter in one place. Gut, viel, gern, hoch, nah, groß and alt. Alt comes from the last lesson: it also gets dots (älter). You can use this table as a cheat sheet. Learn the seven pairs together.
cards.lead: You have met all the special forms one by one. This card puts them in one table, so you can see the whole group, and say them from memory.

examples.de: Die App ist besser als die Zeitung.
examples.en: The app is better than the newspaper.

examples.de: Die Spielkonsole ist größer als das Smartphone.
examples.en: The games console is bigger than the smartphone.

examples.de: Mira hat mehr Kopfhörer als Ben.
examples.en: Mira has more headphones than Ben.

deeper.text: In lesson 3 you will see that these same words also make the superlative: am besten (best), am meisten (most), am liebsten (most gladly). You have already met am liebsten. For now learn them as three whole chunks: they are very common.

example.de: Diese App ist am besten.
example.en: This app is the best.

cards.more: A cheat sheet is a small piece of paper with the most important facts. This table is yours for the chapter. There are seven pairs, and each pair has one short, strong word that you will say a thousand times. Gut, besser. Viel, mehr. Gern, lieber. Hoch, höher. Nah, näher. Groß, größer. Alt, älter. Read the table out loud once a day and in a week it will be in your head.

cards.title: Comparing devices
cards.body: Now put it together. Choose two things, choose an adjective, make the comparative (regular or irregular), and add als. You can also join two comparisons with aber: Das Tablet ist größer, aber das Smartphone ist praktischer.
cards.lead: You have the whole set of forms. On this last card you use them together to compare devices, the real topic of this chapter.

cards.more: Think of a shopping trip. You hold two things and ask three small questions. What are the two things? Which word describes them (big, cheap, good)? What is the form (-er or special)? Then you say it with als. If you want to say both a good and a bad point, you join two sentences with aber, like a seesaw: bigger, but less practical.
steps: Step 1: choose two things: das Tablet and das Smartphone.
Step 2: choose the adjective and make the comparative: groß, größer.
Step 3: join with als: Das Tablet ist größer als das Smartphone.

lessons.title: Am schnellsten, so gut wie: superlative and equal
lessons.goal: Say which one is the best with am ...-sten and say that two things are equal with so ... wie; pronounce b and w.

grammar.point: The winner of three or more is am + adjective + -sten (after t, d, s, z, ß: -esten). Irregular: am besten, am meisten, am liebsten, am höchsten, am nächsten, am größten. Equal: so + adjective + wie.

mistake.right: Die Serie ist so spannend wie der Film.
mistake.why: Als belongs to a comparative with -er. After so or genauso you need wie, and the adjective has no -er.

cards.title: Before we start: the best of all
cards.body: Which app is the best? Which series is as good as the film? You can already say that one thing is better than another. Today you learn two more tools: the winner (am besten) and the tie (so spannend wie). You also practise a few sounds, because b and w are easy to mix up.
steps: You already know: the comparative and als, and the irregular forms besser and mehr.
New today: the winner with am + adjective + -sten, and the tie with so ... wie.
By the end you can: say which one is the best and that two things are equal.

examples.de: Die App ist besser.
examples.en: The app is better.
examples.why: You know this already.

examples.de: Diese App ist am besten.
examples.en: This app is the best.
examples.why: New today: am besten means the best of all.

examples.de: Die Serie ist so spannend wie der Film.
examples.en: The series is as exciting as the film.
examples.why: New today: so ... wie means as ... as.

cards.more: Picture a race. Two runners: one is faster than the other. That is the comparative. Now picture all the runners in a line: only one wins. That one is the fastest of all, am schnellsten. Sometimes two runners cross the line at the same moment: they are equally fast, so schnell wie. In German each of these three ideas has its own small signal: -er and als, am ...-sten, and so ... wie. Today you learn the last two.

cards.title: am ...-sten: the winner
cards.body: To say something is the best of all, put am before the adjective and add -sten: am schnellsten, am kleinsten, am billigsten. After a word ending in -t, -d, -s, -z or -ß add -esten so you can say it: am ältesten, am kürzesten, am berühmtesten. Words ending in -e, like leise, just add -sten: am leisesten.
cards.lead: You know how to say that one thing is more than another. Now you learn the top step, the winner among three or more, so you can say who or what is the best.

examples.de: Ben ist am schnellsten.
examples.en: Ben is the fastest.

examples.de: Das Handy ist am billigsten.
examples.en: The phone is the cheapest.

examples.de: Herr Ali ist am ältesten.
examples.en: Herr Ali is the oldest.

deeper.text: The short words with an Umlaut keep their dots in the winner form: alt, älter, am ältesten. Adjectives ending in -end are a small exception to the e rule: they take only -sten, so spannend becomes am spannendsten, not spannendesten. You can use am ...-sten after ist and also after action verbs: Ben läuft am schnellsten means he runs the fastest.

example.de: Mira läuft am schnellsten.
example.en: Mira runs the fastest.

cards.more: Look at the two letters at the front. Am is a flag that says: this is the winner. Then comes the adjective, and at the end you hang -sten like a medal. When the adjective ends in a hard letter (t, d, s, z), the medal does not fit directly, so a little e goes between them, am ältesten, and your mouth can say it. A common mistake is to forget the n: am schnellste is wrong, am schnellsten is right.

cards.title: Irregular winners
cards.body: The words that are irregular in the comparative are irregular in the winner form too. Gut is am besten, viel is am meisten, gern is am liebsten, hoch is am höchsten, nah is am nächsten, groß is am größten. Learn each as one piece.
cards.lead: The winner form has its own special words too. You have met am besten, am meisten and am liebsten before, and this card adds three more.

examples.de: Diese App ist am besten.
examples.en: This app is the best.

examples.de: Anna liest am meisten.
examples.en: Anna reads the most.

examples.de: Der Turm ist am höchsten.
examples.en: The tower is the highest.

deeper.text: Am nächsten means nearest, and nächsten also appears in der nächste Bus, the next bus. It is the same word: the nearest bus is the next one. Groß is also a small exception to the e rule: it ends in ß, so you would expect am größesten, but German says am größten. Treat am größten as one piece, like the other irregular winners.

example.de: Der Bahnhof ist am nächsten.
example.en: The station is the nearest.

cards.more: These six pairs are the same friends you met last lesson, and now they get a flag, am, and a little tail. Gut, besser, am besten: good, better, best. Viel, mehr, am meisten: much, more, most. Gern, lieber, am liebsten. Hoch, höher, am höchsten. Nah, näher, am nächsten. Groß, größer, am größten. Say each line three times and the whole group will sit in your ear.

cards.title: All three steps in one table
cards.body: You now have three steps of comparing: the basic word (schnell), the comparative (schneller) and the winner (am schnellsten). In this chapter you use the winner only in the form am ...-sten. Other forms, like the fastest film, come in a later chapter.
cards.lead: You have seen each step alone. Here they stand in one table, so you can see how the basic word grows into the winner.

examples.de: Das Handy ist schnell, das Tablet ist schneller, der Laptop ist am schnellsten.
examples.en: The phone is fast, the tablet is faster, the laptop is the fastest.

examples.de: Ben ist alt, Frau Weber ist älter, Herr Ali ist am ältesten.
examples.en: Ben is old, Frau Weber is older, Herr Ali is the oldest.

examples.de: Mira liest viel, Leon liest mehr, Anna liest am meisten.
examples.en: Mira reads a lot, Leon reads more, Anna reads the most.

deeper.text: The winner needs at least three things. With only two things you use the comparative (the faster one), with three or more you can use the winner. German speakers say it the same way you do in English: Of these three, this one is the fastest.

example.de: Ben ist am größten.
example.en: Ben is the tallest.

cards.more: Think of a staircase with three steps. On the first step stands one thing: schnell. On the second step stands a thing that is above it: schneller. On the top step stands the winner: am schnellsten. The staircase is the same for every adjective, only the words change. For the irregular words the steps just have different shapes: gut, besser, am besten. When you build a sentence, ask: how many things do I compare? One alone: basic word. Two: comparative with als. Three or more: am ...-sten.

cards.title: so ... wie: equal
cards.body: To say two things are the same, use so + adjective + wie: Die Serie ist so spannend wie der Film. For just the same, say genauso instead of so. To say not the same, add nicht: nicht so billig wie. The adjective has no -er here.
cards.lead: You can say that one thing is more and that one is the most. Now you learn the third idea, that two things are equal, which you use to say that something is just as good.

examples.de: Die Serie ist so spannend wie der Film.
examples.en: The series is as exciting as the film.

examples.de: Ben ist genauso groß wie Leon.
examples.en: Ben is just as tall as Leon.

examples.de: Mein Handy ist nicht so billig wie dein Handy.
examples.en: My phone is not as cheap as your phone.

deeper.text: Nicht so ... wie says the first thing has less of the quality: Mein Handy ist nicht so billig wie dein Handy means yours is the cheaper one. So you can say less without a new word. Notice too that the adjective stays in its basic form, with no -er.

example.de: Das Tablet ist nicht so teuer wie der Laptop.
example.en: The tablet is not as expensive as the laptop.

cards.more: Imagine two people holding hands at the same height. So ... wie is like a pair of hands: so on one side, wie on the other, and the adjective in between, in its normal form. If you want to say that they are exactly the same, you use genauso, which is like squeezing the hands harder. If one is lower, you say nicht so: not as high. The word after wie is in the nominative, like after als: so alt wie ich.
steps: Step 1: thing 1 + ist: Die Serie ist.
Step 2: so + adjective (no -er): so spannend.
Step 3: wie + thing 2: wie der Film.

cards.title: als or wie?
cards.body: Two small words, two jobs. Use als after a comparative with -er: größer als. Use wie after so or genauso: so groß wie. If you see -er, say als. If you see so, say wie.
cards.lead: You now have two ways of comparing, and two small words that look alike in English. This card helps you pick the right one.

examples.de: Mein Handy ist teurer als dein Handy.
examples.en: My phone is more expensive than your phone.

examples.de: Mein Handy ist so teuer wie dein Handy.
examples.en: My phone is as expensive as your phone.

examples.de: Mein Handy ist nicht so teuer wie dein Handy.
examples.en: My phone is not as expensive as your phone.

deeper.text: Many German speakers say wie where they mean als, especially when they speak fast. In school and in writing it counts as a mistake. A trick: if you can say more or -er in English (bigger than), use als. If you say as ... as, use wie.

example.de: Leon ist lustiger als Ben.
example.en: Leon is funnier than Ben.

cards.more: Als and wie are two doors. The sign on the first door says: -er. If you see an -er word, go through the als door. The sign on the second door says: so. If you see so or genauso, go through the wie door. You cannot walk through both doors in one sentence. English calls them than and as, so they are easy to mix up. German puts the sign right in the sentence: look for -er or so, and you will pick the right word.

rows: Ben ist so groß wie Leon.
Ben ist nicht so groß wie Anna.

cards.title: Sounds: b and w, and word stress
cards.body: B sounds like English b: Bildschirm, besser, beliebt. W sounds like English v: wie, witzig, wir. So Bein (leg) and Wein (wine) sound different. Word stress: most German words stress the first syllable, but words from other languages are often stressed on a later syllable: comPUter, stuDENT.
cards.lead: The chapter is full of words with b and w, and these two letters are easy to mix up. This last card is about sounds, not grammar, and it helps you speak clearly.

examples.de: Wie witzig ist Ben?
examples.en: How funny is Ben?

examples.de: Mein Bildschirm ist besser.
examples.en: My screen is better.

examples.de: Ben ist beliebt, aber Leon ist witziger.
examples.en: Ben is popular, but Leon is funnier.

deeper.text: Say the pair out loud. Bein with b: lips come together and open. Wein with w: your top teeth touch your lower lip, like the English v. Another useful tip: stress is the louder, longer syllable. In BILDschirm and FERNseher it is the first part. In comPUter and restauRANT it is the last part. When you learn a new word, learn its stress too.

example.de: Wir wohnen weit weg.
example.en: We live far away.

cards.more: Your mouth has two ways to start these sounds. For b, close your lips and open them with a small pop, like English baby. For w, do not close your lips: touch your top teeth to your bottom lip and let air through, like English very. Listen to the pairs Bein, Wein and bald, Wald. Stress is the beat of the word: most German words have it on the first part, like HANdy. Words from abroad often have it at the end: comPUter.

lessons.goal: Give and ask for an opinion with finden, denken, glauben, meinen, hoffen + dass, with the verb at the end.

grammar.point: Dass means that. After finden, denken, glauben, meinen and hoffen it starts a side sentence with its own subject. Always put a comma before dass. The conjugated verb goes to the END of the side sentence, just like after weil. Nicht goes before the adjective or before the verb at the end.

mistake.why: After dass the conjugated verb goes to the end of the clause, not into place 2. It works like weil.

terms.meaning: the side sentence that starts with dass (that); its conjugated verb is at the end

cards.title: Before we start: one more word that sends the verb to the end
cards.body: You often say what you think: this phone is too expensive, that series is great. So far you said it in two short sentences: Ich denke, das ist gut. Today you learn a longer and more complete way with the word dass. It works exactly like weil, and you will use it every day.
steps: You already know: Ich denke, das ist gut, and weil with the verb at the end (earlier in this level).
New today: Ich denke, dass das gut ist. The word dass sends the verb to the end.
By the end you can: say and ask opinions with finden, denken, glauben, meinen and hoffen + dass.

examples.de: Ich denke, das ist gut.
examples.en: I think it is good.
examples.why: You know this already: two sentences, the verb stays in place 2.

examples.de: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich müde bin.
examples.en: I stay at home because I am tired.
examples.why: You know this too: after weil the verb goes to the end.

examples.de: Ich denke, dass das gut ist.
examples.en: I think that it is good.
examples.why: New today: after dass the verb ist goes to the end, like after weil.

cards.more: Imagine you tell a friend a secret in two parts. First part: I think. Second part: what you think. In German you can glue the second part to the first with the little word dass, which means that. When you glue it on, the second part gets a small rule: its verb waits until the very end, like a person who is always the last to leave a party. You already did this with weil. Dass is the same trick with a different job: weil gives a reason, dass says what you think.

cards.title: Two ways to give an opinion
cards.body: You know two short sentences in a row: Ich denke, das ist gut. Both parts keep the verb in place 2. The second way is Ich denke, dass das gut ist. The meaning is the same, but after dass the verb jumps to the end. The dass way sounds more complete.
cards.lead: In the introduction you met dass next to a sentence you already know. Here you put the two ways side by side, so you can see exactly what moves when you add dass and what stays the same.

examples.de: Ich denke, dass das gut ist.
examples.en: I think that it is good.
examples.why: The verb ist moved to the end.

examples.de: Ich finde, dass das Handy zu teuer ist.
examples.en: I think the phone is too expensive.

examples.de: Ben denkt, dass die App praktisch ist.
examples.en: Ben thinks that the app is practical.

deeper.text: In English you can drop the word that: I think it is good. German also lets you drop it, but only in the short form without dass. As soon as you write dass, the verb must go to the end. You cannot mix the two ways: dass together with the verb in place 2 is always wrong.

example.de: Ich denke, dass es gut ist.
example.en: I think that it is good.

cards.more: Think of a sentence as a train. In a normal sentence the engine, the verb, rides in the second wagon. When you hang the little word dass behind your first sentence, you start a second small train. In this small train the engine always rides in the very last wagon. So: Ich denke, [dass das gut ist]. The first train keeps its engine in second place. The small train has its engine at the end. If you leave out dass, there is no small train, and the verb stays in its normal place.

headers: with dass: verb at the end

steps: Say the opinion starter: Ich denke,
Add dass: Ich denke, dass
Say the subject and the other words: das gut
Put the conjugated verb at the very end: ist.

cards.title: dass works like weil
cards.body: You know weil from earlier in this level: it starts a side sentence and the verb goes to the end. Dass does exactly the same. There is always a comma in front of it, and the conjugated verb waits at the end. The colours help: dass is a conjunction, the last verb has the verb-end colour.
cards.lead: You have seen that the verb jumps to the end after dass. Now you see why that feels familiar: weil does the same, so you do not have to learn a new rule, only a new word with a new job.

examples.de: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich müde bin.
examples.en: I stay at home because I am tired.
examples.why: weil gives a reason.

examples.de: Ich denke, dass ich müde bin.
examples.en: I think that I am tired.
examples.why: dass says what you think. The shape is the same as with weil.

examples.de: Anna denkt, dass wir heute Zeit haben.
examples.en: Anna thinks that we have time today.
examples.why: haben is the conjugated verb, in last place.

deeper.text: The comma before dass is a hard rule in German. Unlike in English, you never skip it. A good trick is to read aloud and make a tiny pause at the comma. Your voice already tells you: a new small sentence starts here, and its verb will come last.

example.de: Ich denke, dass wir Zeit haben.
example.en: I think that we have time.

cards.more: Many learners forget the comma and write Ich denke dass das gut ist. That is wrong. The right way is Ich denke, dass das gut ist. The comma is like a small door: you close the first sentence and you open the second one. A second mistake is to keep the verb in place 2: Ich denke, dass das ist gut is wrong. After dass the verb goes to the end, so: dass das gut ist. Check both every time: comma first, verb last.

rows: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich müde bin.

cards.title: Opinion verbs: finden, denken, glauben, meinen
cards.body: Four verbs start an opinion. Finden, denken and glauben mean I find, I think and I believe. Meinen means to think, to mean, and it sounds a little stronger. After all four you put a comma and dass. They are regular verbs, so you already know how to conjugate them.
cards.lead: Now you know the shape of a dass sentence. This card gives you the four starters you will use most: you can choose the one that fits how sure you are, and the rest of the sentence stays the same.

examples.de: Ich glaube, dass Ben im Café ist.
examples.en: I believe that Ben is in the café.

examples.de: Mira meint, dass die Pizza zu teuer ist.
examples.en: Mira thinks that the pizza is too expensive.

examples.de: Du denkst, dass Leon müde ist.
examples.en: You think that Leon is tired.

deeper.text: Two more starters are useful. Hoffen means to hope: Ich hoffe, dass du Zeit hast. And Schade, dass es regnet is a ready-made chunk with no first verb at all: it means It is a pity that it is raining. Learn both as pieces. They follow the same rule: comma, dass, verb at the end. Natives use Schade, dass ... all the time to show they are sorry.

example.de: Ich hoffe, dass du Zeit hast.
example.en: I hope that you have time.

cards.more: You already know how these verbs work in the present: ich finde, du findest, er findet. The only new thing is what comes after. Think of the four verbs as four different voices. Finden says I find it so. Denken says I think. Glauben says I believe, and you are not completely sure. Meinen says I mean, and you want others to hear it. After each voice you open the small train with a comma and dass. Hoffen, to hope, is a fifth voice, and you meet it in A bit deeper below.

cards.title: dass with a comparison
cards.body: Opinions often compare things. The comparison stays together inside the dass clause and the verb still goes last: ..., dass Serien spannender als Filme sind. So the order is: subject, the comparison with als, then the verb. Keep the comparison together before the verb.
cards.lead: You have learned the comparative in this chapter, and now you have a place to use it. Your opinions get stronger when you compare, so here you put the comparison inside the dass clause.

examples.de: Ich finde, dass Serien spannender als Filme sind.
examples.en: I think that series are more exciting than films.

examples.de: Ben denkt, dass das Tablet besser als das Handy ist.
examples.en: Ben thinks that the tablet is better than the phone.

examples.de: Anna glaubt, dass Mira mehr Zeit als Ben hat.
examples.en: Anna believes that Mira has more time than Ben.

deeper.text: The whole phrase stays in front of the last verb with the winner and so ... wie, too: Ich finde, dass diese App am besten ist. Natives sometimes also put als and the second thing after the verb: dass Serien spannender sind als Filme. That is correct as well, but it is a spoken habit. Keep the order of this lesson until it feels easy, and you will always be right.

example.de: Ich finde, dass diese App am besten ist.
example.en: I think that this app is the best.

cards.more: Picture the dass clause as a box with the verb as a lid. Everything goes into the box first: who, what and the comparison. Only at the end you close the box with the verb. In ..., dass Serien spannender als Filme sind, the box holds Serien, spannender and als Filme. Then comes sind as the lid. Many learners stop too early and put sind in the middle: dass Serien sind spannender. That is the sentence with the lid in the wrong place. Fill the box first, close it last.

rows: Ich finde, dass Serien spannender als Filme sind.
Das Tablet ist besser als das Handy.
Ben denkt, dass das Tablet besser als das Handy ist.
Mira hat mehr Zeit als Ben.

cards.title: nicht in a dass clause
cards.body: Nicht goes inside the dass clause, in front of the word it makes negative. With an adjective, nicht stands before the adjective: ..., dass Ben nicht online ist. With a verb alone, nicht stands right before the verb at the end: ..., dass Leon nicht arbeitet. The verb stays last.
cards.lead: You can now say what you think. But sometimes you think something is not true, so on this card you learn where nicht goes in a dass clause and why the verb still keeps the last place.

examples.de: Ich glaube, dass Ben nicht online ist.
examples.en: I believe that Ben is not online.

examples.de: Mira findet, dass die App nicht praktisch ist.
examples.en: Mira thinks that the app is not practical.

examples.de: Ich denke, dass Leon nicht arbeitet.
examples.en: I think that Leon is not working.

deeper.text: For a negative opinion you have two choices. You can put nicht inside the clause: Ich glaube, dass Ben nicht online ist. Or you can put nicht in the first sentence: Ich glaube nicht, dass Ben online ist. In everyday talk many people prefer the second way. The next card uses it in answers.

example.de: Ich glaube nicht, dass Ben online ist.
example.en: I do not believe that Ben is online.

cards.more: Nicht is a small stop sign, and it stands right in front of the word it stops. If you want to say that Ben is not online, the stop sign goes in front of online. If you want to say that Leon does not work, there is only the verb, so the stop sign goes in front of the verb, and that is the last word anyway. The verb never moves away from the end because of nicht. In short clauses like these the order is: subject, nicht, adjective or nothing, then the verb.

rows: ..., dass die App nicht praktisch ist.

cards.title: Ask for an opinion: Glaubst du, dass ...?
cards.body: To ask for an opinion, start with a yes-no question and add a dass clause: Glaubst du, dass Leon zu viel online ist? The question verb comes first. After the comma the verb goes to the end. You answer with Ja, ich glaube, dass ... or Nein, ich glaube nicht, dass ...
cards.lead: You can say your opinion and make it negative. The last step is to ask other people: this card gives you the question and the two short answers, so you can have a real opinion conversation.

examples.de: Glaubst du, dass Leon zu viel online ist?
examples.en: Do you believe that Leon is online too much?

examples.de: Ja, ich glaube, dass Leon zu viel online ist.
examples.en: Yes, I believe that Leon is online too much.

examples.de: Nein, ich glaube nicht, dass Leon zu viel online ist.
examples.en: No, I do not believe that Leon is online too much.

deeper.text: You can use every starter you know in a question: Denkst du, dass ...? Findest du, dass ...? Meinst du, dass ...? The answer copies the same dass clause. A very short answer is also fine: Ja, das glaube ich. or Nein, das glaube ich nicht.

example.de: Findest du, dass das Handy teuer ist?
example.en: Do you think the phone is expensive?

cards.more: A question with dass has two parts, like a sandwich. The top slice is your question: Glaubst du, with the verb first because it is a yes-no question. The filling is the dass clause: dass Leon zu viel online ist, with the verb at the end. When you answer, you build the same sandwich again, but with ich in the first part: Ja, ich glaube, dass ... For no, you add nicht after glaube. Keep the filling the same, so you only have to change the top slice.

lessons.title: Ich weiß, dass ...: dass with modals, Perfekt and separable verbs
lessons.goal: Report facts and wishes in long dass sentences with a modal, the Perfekt or a separable verb, put the dass clause first, and tell das from dass.

grammar.point: After wissen, sagen, es ist wichtig and ich bin sicher the dass clause works as before. With a modal the infinitive stands before the modal at the very end (kochen kann). In the Perfekt the participle stands before hat or ist (gepostet hat). A separable verb stays in one piece (herunterlädt). The dass clause can come first: then the main verb follows the comma at once. Das is an article or pronoun, dass is the conjunction.
grammar.oneLine: Ich weiß, dass Ben das Video hochgeladen hat. Dass du ständig online bist, finde ich nicht gut.

mistake.wrong: Ich weiß, dass Ben hat das Video hochgeladen.
mistake.right: Ich weiß, dass Ben das Video hochgeladen hat.
mistake.why: In a dass clause the helper verb goes to the very end, after the participle.

terms.meaning: a helper verb such as können, müssen, dürfen, wollen; in a dass clause it is the last word
the form for the Perfekt, for example gepostet or gesehen
a verb with a front part that splits off in a normal sentence, for example herunterladen

cards.title: Before we start: the verb at the end, the long version
cards.body: Last time you said what you think: Ich glaube, dass Ben online ist. But real sentences are longer. Ben has uploaded a video, Mira can cook, Leon downloads an app. Today you learn what happens to these longer verbs inside a dass clause. The rule is easy: everything goes into the clause first, and the verbs close it.
steps: You already know: Ich glaube, dass Ben online ist. One verb at the end.
New today: dass clauses with a modal verb, with the Perfekt and with a separable verb, and the starters Ich weiß, ...
By the end you can: report facts and wishes in long dass sentences, and tell das from dass.

examples.de: Ich glaube, dass Ben online ist.
examples.en: I believe that Ben is online.
examples.why: You know this already: one verb at the end.

examples.de: Ich weiß, dass Ben das Video hochgeladen hat.
examples.en: I know that Ben has uploaded the video.
examples.why: New today: two verbs at the end. The helper verb hat is the very last word.

cards.more: In the last lesson the end of the dass clause had one verb, like one small door at the end of a hall. Today some halls have two doors. When you use the Perfekt or a modal, two verbs wait at the end. The rule for the order is simple and always the same: the verb that changes with the person (hat, kann) takes the very last place, and the other one, the participle or the infinitive, stands right in front of it. Learn that and you can build very long sentences.

cards.title: More starters: wissen, sagen, es ist wichtig
cards.body: Not only opinion verbs open a dass clause. Wissen (to know), sagen (to say), Es ist wichtig, ... and Ich bin sicher, ... also take dass. The rule stays the same: comma, dass, verb at the end. Wissen is irregular: ich weiß, du weißt, er weiß.
cards.lead: You know how dass works after finden and glauben. This card shows more openers, so you can also report facts and say what matters, and the clause after them follows the same rule.

examples.de: Ich weiß, dass Ben heute Zeit hat.
examples.en: I know that Ben has time today.

examples.de: Leon sagt, dass er müde ist.
examples.en: Leon says that he is tired.

examples.de: Es ist wichtig, dass du kommst.
examples.en: It is important that you come.

deeper.text: Wissen is easy to mix up with kennen. Both mean to know in English, but German keeps them apart. Use wissen for facts and whole statements, so it is the one that takes dass: Ich weiß, dass Anna kommt. Use kennen for people and places you are familiar with: Ich kenne Anna. In short answers natives also say just Ich weiß or Weiß ich nicht, with no dass at all.

example.de: Ich kenne Anna, und ich weiß, dass sie kommt.
example.en: I know Anna, and I know that she is coming.

cards.more: Think of the starter as the title of a news report. Ich weiß says: here is something I know. Er sagt says: here is what someone told me. Es ist wichtig says: here is something that matters. Ich bin sicher says: I am very sure of this. After the title you always open the little train with a comma and dass, and its engine, the verb, rides in the last wagon. Only the title changes. The rest of the sentence you already know how to build.

rows: Ich weiß, dass Ben Zeit hat.
Er sagt, dass er müde ist.
Es ist wichtig, dass du kommst.
Ich bin sicher, dass Anna heute arbeitet.

cards.title: dass with a modal verb
cards.body: With a modal verb the dass clause has two verbs. The infinitive stands first, and the modal is the very last word: ..., dass Mira gut kochen kann. The infinitive has the second-verb colour, the modal has the verb-end colour.
cards.lead: You know modal verbs and you know that the verb goes to the end after dass. Here the two ideas meet: this card shows the order of the two verbs, so you always know which one comes last.

examples.de: Ich weiß, dass Mira gut kochen kann.
examples.en: I know that Mira can cook well.

examples.de: Ben sagt, dass er heute nicht kommen kann.
examples.en: Ben says that he cannot come today.

examples.de: Ich glaube, dass wir das Video heute sehen können.
examples.en: I believe that we can see the video today.

deeper.text: What about nicht? With two verbs at the end, nicht stands in front of the infinitive, so just before the verb group: Ben sagt, dass er nicht kommen kann. You do not put nicht between the two verbs. The same order works in a weil clause from earlier in this level. Always read the end of the clause as one block: nicht, infinitive, modal.

example.de: Ich weiß, dass Mira nicht singen kann.
example.en: I know that Mira cannot sing.

cards.more: Imagine two people leaving a room through a narrow door. The one with the strong person ending, the modal, always leaves last, like a host who closes the door. The other one, the infinitive, goes right before. So you say kochen kann, not kann kochen. In a normal sentence the modal has place 2 and the infinitive is at the end: Mira kann gut kochen. In a dass clause the modal moves to the very end and the infinitive stays right in front of it.

rows: Ich weiß, dass Mira gut kochen kann.
Anna sagt, dass Ben heute arbeiten muss.
Ich hoffe, dass wir einen Film sehen können.

cards.title: dass with the Perfekt
cards.body: In the Perfekt the participle stands before the helper verb, and the helper verb hat or ist is the very last word: ..., dass er das Video gepostet hat. The participle has the second-verb colour, the helper has the verb-end colour. Never forget the helper at the end.
cards.lead: You can build the Perfekt in a normal sentence. In a dass clause the two parts swap places: this card shows the new order so you can talk about the past in long sentences.

examples.de: Ben sagt, dass er das Video gepostet hat.
examples.en: Ben says that he has posted the video.

examples.de: Ich weiß, dass Mira gestern einen Film gesehen hat.
examples.en: I know that Mira saw a film yesterday.

examples.de: Anna glaubt, dass Leon nach Hause gegangen ist.
examples.en: Anna believes that Leon has gone home.

deeper.text: Which helper do you put last, hat or ist? Most verbs take hat: gepostet hat, gesehen hat. Verbs of movement and change of state, and bleiben, take ist: gegangen ist, geblieben ist, gefahren ist. The helper is the verb that changes with the person, so after dass it is the last word: ..., dass wir gegangen sind. A clause that ends on the participle alone is not finished.

example.de: Ich weiß, dass Anna zu Hause geblieben ist.
example.en: I know that Anna stayed at home.

cards.more: In a normal Perfekt sentence the helper verb is in place 2, and the participle is at the end: Ben hat das Video gepostet. Think of two friends walking. The helper verb walks in front. After dass the order is turned around: the participle walks in front and the helper comes last. Same two words, new order. If you see dass, look for the helper at the very end, like a full stop. Always check: have I put hat or ist at the end?

rows: Ben sagt, dass er das Video gepostet hat.
Ich weiß, dass Mira einen Film gesehen hat.
Anna glaubt, dass Leon nach Hause gegangen ist.

cards.title: dass with a separable verb
cards.body: A separable verb splits in a normal sentence: Leon lädt die App herunter. In a dass clause it stays in one piece at the end: ..., dass Leon die App herunterlädt. The two parts join and the whole word has the verb-end colour.
cards.lead: You know that separable verbs split into two parts. After dass they do not split at all, because the verb is already at the end. This card shows the joined form.

examples.de: Ich glaube, dass Leon die App herunterlädt.
examples.en: I believe that Leon downloads the app.

examples.de: Ben sagt, dass er morgen früh aufsteht.
examples.en: Ben says that he gets up early tomorrow.

examples.de: Ich weiß, dass Anna heute einkauft.
examples.en: I know that Anna is shopping today.

deeper.text: If the separable verb is in the Perfekt, the participle stands in front of the helper as usual: dass Ben das Video hochgeladen hat. With a modal the separable verb stays in the infinitive, in one piece: dass Leon die App herunterladen kann.

example.de: Ich weiß, dass Leon die App herunterladen kann.
example.en: I know that Leon can download the app.

cards.more: A separable verb is like a pair of magnets. In a normal sentence they pull apart: lädt ... herunter, one part in place 2 and one at the end. At the end of a dass clause there is no more room to pull apart, because the verb is already at the end. So the magnets snap together: herunterlädt. You write them as one word. Say it as one word, too. The joined verb is simply the verb at the end.

cards.title: The dass clause first
cards.body: You can also start the sentence with the dass clause. Then the main clause follows with its verb first: Dass du ständig online bist, finde ich nicht gut. Look at the middle: a verb, a comma, and at once the next verb. This is verb, comma, verb.
cards.lead: Until now the dass clause always came second. This card shows a version where it comes first, useful when you want to stress the idea. The rule for the verbs makes this look strange at first, so you see it step by step.

examples.de: Dass du ständig online bist, finde ich nicht gut.
examples.en: That you are online all the time, I do not like.

examples.de: Dass Ben viel streamt, weiß ich.
examples.en: That Ben streams a lot, I know.

examples.de: Dass Mira gut kochen kann, finde ich super.
examples.en: That Mira can cook well, I think is great.

deeper.text: The dass clause in first place can also be the subject of a short sentence. Dass du kommst, ist toll means That you are coming is great. Here the whole dass clause does the job of one word, like a subject. The verb ist follows right after the comma, in place 2. This is a favourite way for natives to react to news. Try it with ist toll, ist schön or ist wichtig.

example.de: Dass du kommst, ist toll.
example.en: That you are coming is great.

cards.more: Most of the time you will say Ich glaube, dass ... and that is perfectly normal. The dass clause first is a style choice, a way to put the idea on a stage in front of everybody. Use it when you want to stress it. Because the whole block stands in place 1, the next word must be the verb of the main sentence. You hear verb, comma, verb in the middle, for example bist, finde. Read it aloud once and you will recognise it later.

rows: Ich weiß, dass Ben viel streamt.
Dass Ben viel streamt, weiß ich.
Ich glaube, dass Mira gut kochen kann.
Dass Mira gut kochen kann, glaube ich.
Ich weiß, dass du ständig online bist.
Dass du ständig online bist, weiß ich.

cards.title: das or dass?
cards.body: Das and dass sound the same but are different words. Das is an article or a pronoun: das Video, Das ist gut. Dass is a conjunction: it comes after a comma and sends the verb to the end. A quick test: if dieses or welches fits, it is das. If not, it is dass.
cards.lead: You have used dass a lot now, and you also know das from the first lessons. This card gives you a test to tell them apart, because they sound the same and a wrong spelling is a very common mistake.

examples.de: Das Video ist lang.
examples.en: The video is long.

examples.de: Ich weiß, dass das Video lang ist.
examples.en: I know that the video is long.
examples.why: One dass and one das in the same sentence.

examples.de: Ich glaube, dass er kommt.
examples.en: I believe that he is coming.

deeper.text: Before the spelling reform of 1996 the conjunction was written daß, with the old ß. Since then it is dass with double s, so older books and letters from your grandparents may look different. The reform made the sound rule clearer: ß after a long vowel, ss after a short one, and dass has a short a. It is still a different word from das, so the test with dieses stays useful.

example.de: Ich glaube, dass das Tablet neu ist.
example.en: I believe that the tablet is new.

cards.more: Two words that sound the same, but they do different jobs. Das is a small pointing word: it points at a thing, like das Video or this thing here. Dass is a connecting word: it connects two parts of a sentence and sends the verb to the end. A common mistake is to write das after the comma: Ich glaube, das er kommt is wrong. It must be Ich glaube, dass er kommt. If you can say dieses instead, write das. If not, write dass.

lessons.title: Immer online? Pros and cons
lessons.goal: Name pros and cons with Ein Vorteil ist, dass ... and Ein Nachteil ist, dass ..., use man and comparisons in dass clauses, agree or disagree, and plan a short text.

grammar.point: Ein Vorteil ist, dass ... and Ein Nachteil ist, dass ... open a dass clause with the verb at the end. Man (one, people) takes the er/sie form. A comparison stays inside the dass clause before the end verb. To agree say Ich glaube auch, dass ...; to disagree put nicht in the first part: Ich glaube nicht, dass ...
grammar.oneLine: Ein Vorteil ist, dass man immer erreichbar ist. Ein Nachteil ist, dass man nicht abschalten kann.

mistake.wrong: Ein Vorteil ist, dass man ist immer erreichbar.
mistake.right: Ein Vorteil ist, dass man immer erreichbar ist.
mistake.why: After dass the conjugated verb goes to the end of the clause, also after Ein Vorteil ist.

terms.meaning: advantage / disadvantage, the good side and the bad side of something
one, people in general; it takes the same verb ending as er or sie
a short phrase that you learn as one piece, for example Moment mal!

cards.title: Before we start: good and bad sides
cards.body: Is it good to be online all the time? Most people say: yes and no. To talk about this you name good sides and bad sides, and you react to other people. Today you put your dass sentences to work, and you learn four small phrases that make a conversation sound natural.
steps: You already know: Ein Vorteil ist: ... (earlier in this level) and dass clauses with the verb at the end.
New today: Ein Vorteil ist, dass ... and Ein Nachteil ist, dass ..., and short phrases like Moment mal!
By the end you can: name two pros and two cons, agree or disagree, and plan a short pro and con text.

examples.de: Ein Vorteil ist: Man ist immer erreichbar.
examples.en: An advantage is: one is always reachable.
examples.why: You know this already: two short sentences.

examples.de: Ich weiß, dass Ben das Video hochgeladen hat.
examples.en: I know that Ben has uploaded the video.
examples.why: You know this too: a dass clause with the verb at the end.

examples.de: Ein Vorteil ist, dass man immer erreichbar ist.
examples.en: An advantage is that one is always reachable.
examples.why: New today: the same idea in one sentence with dass.

cards.more: Imagine a set of scales. On the left plate you put the good sides of something, on the right plate the bad sides. In German you have two small openers for the two plates: Ein Vorteil ist, dass ... for the good side and Ein Nachteil ist, dass ... for the bad side. Both open a dass clause, and you already know how that works. So today you do not need a new rule. You only need two new openers and a few phrases to talk with other people.

cards.title: Ein Vorteil ist, dass ... and Ein Nachteil ist, dass ...
cards.body: To name a good side say Ein Vorteil ist, dass ... To name a bad side say Ein Nachteil ist, dass ... The first part is a short sentence with ist. After the comma comes the dass clause with the verb at the end. There is nothing new in the rule, only the opener is new.
cards.lead: You know Vorteil and Nachteil as words. Now you use them to open a dass clause, which gives you a very clear way to list the good and bad sides of any topic in complete sentences.

examples.de: Ein Vorteil ist, dass man immer erreichbar ist.
examples.en: An advantage is that one is always reachable.

examples.de: Ein Nachteil ist, dass man ständig Werbung sieht.
examples.en: A disadvantage is that one sees advertising all the time.

examples.de: Ein Nachteil ist, dass Ben ständig online ist.
examples.en: A disadvantage is that Ben is online all the time.

deeper.text: You can also use the with a noun that you have already named: Der Vorteil ist, dass ... But when you list several points, ein is better, because it says: this is one of the advantages. The dass clause always follows the same pattern: subject, other words, verb at the end.

example.de: Der Nachteil ist, dass der Akku schnell leer ist.
example.en: The disadvantage is that the battery runs down quickly.

cards.more: Think of a list with two columns. Above the left column there is a plus sign: Ein Vorteil ist, dass ... Above the right column there is a minus sign: Ein Nachteil ist, dass ... Under each sign you write full dass sentences. The rule is the same for both columns, so you only have to swap one word: Vorteil or Nachteil. Everything after the comma is a normal dass clause: who, what, and at the end the verb. If you can build one sentence, you can build ten.

rows: Ein Vorteil ist, dass man schnell Informationen findet.
Ein Nachteil ist, dass man ständig Werbung sieht.
Ein Vorteil ist, dass das WLAN schnell ist.
Ein Nachteil ist, dass der Akku schnell leer ist.
Ein Vorteil ist, dass Mira immer erreichbar ist.
Ein Nachteil ist, dass sie nie offline ist.

steps: Start with the opener: Ein Vorteil ist, (or Ein Nachteil ist,)
Add dass: ... ist, dass
Say who and what: man schnell Informationen
Put the verb at the end: findet.

cards.title: man in dass clauses
cards.body: Man means one or people in general. It is very useful for pros and cons, because you talk about everybody, not about one person. Man always takes the er/sie form: man findet, man kann, man ist. In a dass clause man is the subject, and the verb waits at the end.
cards.lead: In a list of pros and cons you often talk about everybody. German has a handy small word for that, and you already know it from earlier chapters. Here you use it inside a dass clause.

examples.de: Ein Vorteil ist, dass man schnell Informationen findet.
examples.en: An advantage is that one finds information quickly.

examples.de: Ich glaube, dass man im Internet viel lernen kann.
examples.en: I believe that one can learn a lot on the internet.

examples.de: Ein Nachteil ist, dass man nicht abschalten kann.
examples.en: A disadvantage is that one cannot switch off.

deeper.text: Man is always singular, even when you mean many people: man kann, not man können. Do not mix it up with the noun der Mann, which is a male person and has two n and a capital letter. The small word man has one n and no capital letter inside a sentence.

example.de: Man kann im Café surfen.
example.en: One can surf in the café.

cards.more: Man is a word for everybody and nobody in particular. In English you say one or you or people: you can learn a lot on the internet. German says man, and the verb goes with er/sie: man kann, man findet, man ist. In a dass clause man is the subject, so the verb stays at the end as usual. You can replace ich with man to make a general statement instead of a personal one. Compare: Ich bin immer erreichbar means me. Man ist immer erreichbar means anyone.

rows: ..., dass man im Internet lernen kann.

cards.title: A comparison inside the dass clause
cards.body: You can mix both tools from this chapter. Ich finde, dass man offline ruhiger ist. Ich glaube, dass Kinder heute mehr Bildschirmzeit als früher haben. The comparison stays inside the clause, and the verb is last. Remember: mehr and weniger never get an ending.
cards.lead: You have the comparative and you have dass. Now you combine them, which is exactly what you need to compare the world with and without a phone, and the verb still has to wait at the end.

examples.de: Ich finde, dass man offline ruhiger ist.
examples.en: I think that one is calmer offline.

examples.de: Ich glaube, dass Kinder heute mehr Bildschirmzeit als früher haben.
examples.en: I believe that children have more screen time today than before.

examples.de: Ben findet, dass Bücher besser als Apps sind.
examples.en: Ben thinks that books are better than apps.

deeper.text: Two time words fit nicely with comparisons: früher means in the past and heutzutage means nowadays. They stand inside the dass clause, before the comparison words. Mehr and weniger never take an ending: mehr Zeit, weniger Zeit. In the colour code they count as adjectives, because they say how much of the noun there is. Together they let you contrast then and now in one sentence.

example.de: Ich glaube, dass man heutzutage weniger Zeit hat.
example.en: I believe that one has less time nowadays.

cards.more: Imagine the comparison as a small seesaw inside your dass box. On the left you put what you compare, on the right the other thing, and als is the pivot in the middle. The seesaw sits inside the box, and the lid, the verb, closes it at the end. Ich glaube, dass Kinder heute mehr Bildschirmzeit als früher haben. Heute and früher are the two sides of the seesaw. If you remember the lid, you cannot go wrong.

rows: Ben findet, dass Bücher besser als Apps sind.
Ich finde, dass man offline ruhiger ist.
Kinder haben heute mehr Bildschirmzeit als früher.
Ich glaube, dass Kinder heute mehr Bildschirmzeit als früher haben.

cards.title: Agree and disagree with dass
cards.body: To agree, repeat the idea and add auch: Ich glaube auch, dass ... To disagree, put nicht in the first part: Ich glaube nicht, dass ... The dass clause itself stays positive. You also know chunks from earlier: Da hast du recht. Das sehe ich anders.
cards.lead: In a conversation you do not only give your own opinion, you also react to others. This card shows how to say yes or no to someone else's idea with the dass pattern you already know.

examples.de: Ich glaube auch, dass man offline ruhiger ist.
examples.en: I also believe that one is calmer offline.

examples.de: Ich glaube nicht, dass man immer erreichbar sein muss.
examples.en: I do not believe that one has to be reachable all the time.

examples.de: Ich stimme dir zu, ich glaube auch, dass Bücher besser als Apps sind.
examples.en: I agree with you, I also believe that books are better than apps.

deeper.text: For a more serious discussion natives use a longer opener: Ich bin der Meinung, dass ... It means I am of the opinion that ..., and it opens a dass clause just like Ich glaube, dass ... You can also agree or disagree with it: Ich bin auch der Meinung, dass ... or Ich bin nicht der Meinung, dass ... Learn Ich bin der Meinung as one piece; the grammar behind der Meinung comes later.

example.de: Ich bin der Meinung, dass man offline ruhiger ist.
example.en: I am of the opinion that one is calmer offline.

cards.more: Think of two small switches. The first switch is auch: it says I agree, me too. The second switch is nicht: it says I do not agree. Both go into the first part of the sentence, right after the verb: Ich glaube auch, ... or Ich glaube nicht, ... The dass clause that follows stays the same. You can copy the idea of your friend and only flip one switch. That makes agreeing and disagreeing very easy.

rows: Ich glaube auch, dass man offline ruhiger ist.
Ich glaube nicht, dass man offline ruhiger ist.
Ich finde auch, dass Serien spannend sind.
Ich finde nicht, dass Serien spannend sind.
Ich denke auch, dass das Handy nützlich ist.
Ich denke nicht, dass das Handy nützlich ist.

cards.title: Small phrases for real talk
cards.body: In a conversation people use small chunks. Habt ihr Zeit? asks if a group is free. Warte mal! and Moment mal! mean wait a moment and stop someone. Na ja ... shows that you are not fully convinced. Learn them as whole pieces, not word by word.
cards.lead: Good conversations are full of short phrases that are not about grammar at all. This card gives you four of them, shown in a short flat-share dialogue, so you can use them as they are.

examples.de: Habt ihr Zeit?
examples.en: Do you (all) have time?

examples.de: Moment mal! Ich glaube nicht, dass das stimmt.
examples.en: Hold on! I do not believe that this is true.

examples.de: Na ja, das ist nicht ganz falsch.
examples.en: Well, that is not completely wrong.

deeper.text: Warte mal! speaks to one person (du). For a group you say Wartet mal! Moment mal! works for one or for many people. Na ja is a small pause word, like well in English. People often say it before they disagree politely or when they only half agree.

example.de: Wartet mal!
example.en: Wait a moment, all of you!

cards.more: These four phrases are like small pieces of glue in a conversation. Habt ihr Zeit? opens the door: you ask if people have a moment. Warte mal! and Moment mal! are stop signs, used when you want to say something or when you do not agree. Na ja is a soft cloud: you are not sure, not fully convinced. You do not translate them word by word. You say them as whole pieces, with the right melody, and everybody understands.

rows: you ask if the group is free
you stop one person for a moment
you stop someone, often because you disagree

steps: Ben: Habt ihr Zeit? Ich möchte etwas zeigen.
Leon: Warte mal! Ich muss noch kurz arbeiten.
Mira: Moment mal! Ich glaube, dass wir alle Zeit haben.
Anna: Na ja, ich bin müde, aber ich komme.

cards.title: Plan a pro and con list in four steps
cards.body: Before you speak or write, plan a list. Step 1: the topic. Step 2: two pros with Ein Vorteil ist, dass ... Step 3: two cons with Ein Nachteil ist, dass ... Step 4: your own opinion with weil. This is the pattern for a good short text.
cards.lead: You now have all the pieces: the openers, man, comparisons and agreeing. This last card puts them in order, so you have a small recipe for a short text about any topic.

examples.de: Ein Vorteil ist, dass man mit Freunden sprechen kann.
examples.en: An advantage is that one can talk with friends.

examples.de: Ein Nachteil ist, dass man schlecht abschalten kann.
examples.en: A disadvantage is that one cannot switch off well.

examples.de: Ich finde das Internet nützlich, weil ich viel lernen kann.
examples.en: I find the internet useful because I can learn a lot.

deeper.text: Join a pro and a con with aber: Ein Vorteil ist, dass man immer erreichbar ist, aber ein Nachteil ist, dass man nicht abschalten kann. Aber is a connector that does not change the order, so the second part has its normal word order, with ist after ein Nachteil.

example.de: Aber ein Nachteil ist, dass man nicht abschalten kann.
example.en: But a disadvantage is that one cannot switch off.

cards.more: A good short text is like a sandwich with four layers. The first layer is the topic: what are we talking about? The second layer holds two pros, the third layer two cons. The last layer is the top slice, your own opinion, and you add the reason with weil. When you have the four layers, writing is just filling in sentences you already know: Ein Vorteil ist, dass ... Ein Nachteil ist, dass ... Ich finde ..., weil ... You cannot get lost.
